extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, judges, and law students
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating whether an improvement, process, material substitution, or new use qualifies as a patentable invention (novelty and substantive invention). Contains doctrinal tests, evidentiary rules, and illustrative case examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: The invention must be new; alleged anticipatory evidence must be strong and conclusive to justify holding a patent void for want of novelty. The grant (and any extension) creates a presumption in favor of novelty and validity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text emphasizes that evidence to impeach novelty 'must be strong and conclusive,' because the presumption of law favors the patentee (from grant and from extension proceedings). Where a patent has been extended after scrutiny, it has very strong presumptive claims to validity. Use of historical/prior-publication or prior-use evidence must be examined carefully and convincingly to overcome this presumption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application of an old thing to a new use (double use)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying a known article or process to a new use may be patentable (a 'discovery' applied to a new object), but whether it is patentable depends on circumstances and the pleadings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by annealing applied to car wheels: annealing was old, but its application to car wheels was held new and patentable because it solved a difficulty specific to that art. Courts will consider whether the old thing, when applied to the new use, exhibits any new combination, effect, or practical result that constitutes invention. Whether to decide such issues may depend on the pleadings and factual record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Changes of mere manufacture, taste, or skill are not invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Changes like a different color, mere change of material, change in degree of fineness, or other alterations that do not involve new construction, relation of parts, or change in office/function do not constitute invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From Smith v. Elliott: superior skill or improved finish that leaves the construction and relation of parts unchanged is typically treated as workmanship or improvement in manufacture, not patentable invention. Evaluate whether the change alters construction, part relations, or function; if not, treat as non-inventive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cheapness or superiority of material is not by itself patentable
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere quality of cheapness or other superiority in the material, disconnected from any new or different mode of applying that material in the process of making the thing, has not been held to be patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However, courts have used superior quality or reduced cost of the product as evidence that a claimed process differs substantively from prior methods (see Crane, Lord Dudley). If the substitution of material leads to a new construction, new mode of operation, or new application of properties, it can be patentable. So treat cheapness as evidentiary (tending to show a substantive change) but not as a standalone ground for patentability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substitution of one material for another — when patentable
rubrics_metrics.description: Simply making the same machine or article out of a different material (e.g., iron instead of wood) that produces the same result in the same way is not invention, unless the substitution involves new attachment/construction, a new mode of operation, or a new application of material properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: If substitution requires a new method of attachment or produces a different mode of operation (or develops new applications of material properties), that specific mode or application can be patentable. Conversely, where any competent constructor could make the substitution using ordinary skill, it is not patentable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of different motive power not normally patentable
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying horse, water, or steam power to a machine previously moved by hand, where the change is within ordinary knowledge and skill, is not patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lowell, J.'s statement: 'The mere means of giving motion to a machine would not ordinarily be a part of the essence of the machine.' Evaluate whether replacing the power source requires inventive skill beyond ordinary practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Process-class inventions: test is the improved effect produced
rubrics_metrics.description: For inventions that consist of substituting one thing for another or adding/omitting steps in a process, the test of patentable novelty is whether the new combination or change produces a new article, a better article, or a cheaper article — i.e., an improved effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Crane v. Price: when known things act together to produce effects as before but in a way that is more economically or beneficially enjoyed by the public, examine whether the result (new/better/cheaper product) indicates a substantive change in process. Courts may treat the improved product as proof the process is novel. Focus on whether the process change produces materially different practical results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omission or reordering of steps can be patentable
rubrics_metrics.description: The omission of an ingredient or a previously-used step, or changing the order of process steps, may constitute patentable invention if it results in a new or improved means of producing the desired effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: patents held valid where cloth was made without an ingredient formerly thought essential; rendering fabric water-proof by immersing in solutions in a new order; Booth v. Kennard where saving one step (making gas directly from seeds rather than extracting oils first) was held a substantive invention. Evaluate whether the omission or reorder materially changes the process or results.

rubrics_metrics.name: New application of known agents leading to new effect is patentable
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying known agents or things in a new way that changes the series of processes to produce a new effect, result, or manufacture can be patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two classes noted: (a) new application of known agents changing process series to produce different effects; (b) discovery and application of new agents producing new effects. Distinguish mere repetition of an old process from genuinely new application to different substrate or context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Material/factual questions determine patentability in some borderline cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a claimed application of a process to a different substance is patentable may depend on factual questions (e.g., whether 'spent madder' is chemically or practically a different substance from 'fresh madder').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts should direct juries to find facts such as chemical differences or prior knowledge in the art; the patentable character should not be drawn as a narrow legal inference when material factual disputes exist. Treat such distinctions as questions of fact material to validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial success, long practice, and diligence are evidentiary supports
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence that the patentee practiced the invention successfully for many years, produced and sold large quantities, and used diligence in bringing the invention to public use strengthens the presumption of novelty and validity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In extension and validity inquiries, the statute and courts look to whether the invention 'had proved of great practical utility to the public' and the patentee used proper diligence. Such practical success is relevant and supportive evidence, though not dispositive by itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: When a process produces a materially different product ('new metal' etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claimed process produces a product that is materially different in properties (e.g., a 'new metal') — by reason of superior properties or cheapness — that fact strongly supports treating the process as patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Crane and Sturz cases: courts sometimes justified patentability on the ground that the product resulting from the new process was effectively new (different in quality or cost). Evaluate product-level differences as a significant indicium of inventive novelty.
